Article Title: 'O Captain, My Captain': Should Congress make room for Amarinder Singh again?
Article Text:
Rahul Gandhi named Captain Amarinder Singh as his favourite BJP leader.

Amarinder Singh on his relationship with Congress leadership.

The 'Uncle Amarinder' connection

Amarinder's BJP discontent

The political career of Captain Amarinder Singh.

From a 77-seat victory to a bitter exit

Sachin Pilot kept the door open to Amarinder Singh's return to the Congress.

Pargat Singh's leadership test

No CM face, but several leadership questions

In June, Amarinder Singh shared that Rahul Gandhi wished him on his birthday.

What could Captain Amarinder's return mean

NEW DELHI: Can a party install a new captain, retain the old team and still leave the door open for a former captain who quit the dressing room five years ago? With the leadership chanting 'O Captain! My Captain!' the Punjab Congress seems to be attempting to navigate that question precisely ahead of the 2027 assembly elections.With Pargat Singh at the helm, Raja Warring and Charanjit Singh Channi 'promised' an active role in the campaign; Sachin Pilot has also left the door open to Captain Amarinder Singh 's possible return. Can Congress accommodate its old captain without unsettling the new captain and the team?Congress general secretary Sachin Pilot, the party's Punjab in-charge, on October 15 offered a line that will keep speculation alive: "Politics mein 'kuch bhi ho sakta hai' (anything is possible in politics)."Asked about the possibility of former Punjab chief minister Captain Amarinder Singh returning to Congress, Pilot praised him as a leader who had served Punjab "well" and was "a man of a very tall stature". He clarified, however, that he had not spoken to Captain Amarinder about his political plans."I've not spoken to him personally about what his future plans are about joining or leaving any party," Pilot told PTI Videos.The remark came less than a fortnight after Congress appointed former India hockey captain Pargat Singh as Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee (PPCC) president, replacing Amrinder Singh Raja Warring on October 2. It also followed Amarinder's public criticism of the BJP, the party he joined in 2022, over its handling of Punjab.So, is Congress merely acknowledging political speculation, or could the old captain's name return to the party's calculations? And if he does return, where would he fit in a state unit that has just changed leadership and is yet to name a CM face?The latest speculation began with an unexpected public greeting. On August 6, during an Instagram 'Ask Me Anything' session with students, leader of the opposition Rahul Gandhi was asked to name his favourite BJP politician."Captain Amarinder Singh, definitely. I get along with him, he's cool and he is an expert on military history, so I like him quite a lot," Rahul Gandhi said, before adding: "Hello, Uncle Amarinder!"The former CM responded that his personal relationship with the Gandhi family would remain, but his political commitment was to the BJP. In a September interview with The Tribune, he said he remained fond of Rahul, Priyanka and Sonia Gandhi, while distinguishing personal relationships from politics."My personal relationship with the Gandhis will always be there, but my political commitment is to the BJP," he said."If tomorrow I tell Rahul, Priyanka or Sonia personally that I'll be there for them no matter what, I mean it and I'm happy to help," he added.The indirect exchange was notable because Amarinder Singh's departure from Congress in September 2021 followed a bitter confrontation with the party's state leadership. "When you've been with somebody for fifty years, they remain your party. I never asked to leave them; they asked me to leave," Captain Amarinder Singh said recently.The former chief minister's recent criticism of the BJP has provided the immediate backdrop to the comeback speculation.In an interview published by The Tribune on September 25, Amarinder said the BJP had not consulted him on Punjab politics or policy despite his long experience in the state."I haven't had a single meeting on Punjab policy or politics with them in the last five years," he said.He was more direct about his decision to join the party: "I have gained nothing by joining BJP."Amarinder also argued that the BJP did not adequately understand Punjab and should consult leaders familiar with the state's political and social realities. He advocated an alliance with the Shiromani Akali Dal, pointing to the BJP's historical position as the junior partner in that relationship.In the same interview, he described himself as going through "difficult times", without elaborating.Yet he has also made clear that dissatisfaction does not automatically mean departure. Amarinder Singh said it was his duty to tell the BJP what he thought about Punjab and that criticising the party's approach did not mean he was quitting.Captain Amarinder Singh's record in Congress spans decades, including two terms as Punjab CM, from 2002 to 2007 and from 2017 to 2021.In the 2017 assembly election, Congress won 77 of Punjab's 117 seats under his leadership, returning to power after a decade. But the relationship between Amarinder Singh and the state leadership deteriorated, particularly amid his prolonged confrontation with Navjot Singh Sidhu.Sidhu became Punjab Congress president in July 2021. The conflict intensified over leadership and the government's handling of election promises. On September 18, 2021, Amarinder resigned as chief minister after the Congress high command called a meeting of the party's legislators to discuss leadership.He subsequently left Congress and launched the Punjab Lok Congress (PLC). In the 2022 assembly election, the PLC allied with the BJP, but the alliance failed to win a seat for Amarinder Singh's party. AAP swept the election with 92 seats, while Congress was reduced to 18.Amarinder joined the BJP in September 2022, and his PLC was merged with it.The electoral record provides the context for the renewed speculation, but it does not establish that bringing Amarinder back would reverse Congress's fortunes. The party's 2022 defeat followed a wider political shift in Punjab, including AAP's rise and Congress's internal divisions.Meanwhile, Pargat Singh's appointment has put a new leader at the head of a state unit that has repeatedly struggled with factional disputes. A former India hockey captain and three-time MLA from Jalandhar Cantonment, he was associated with Sidhu during the 2021 confrontation with Amarinder Singh and had publicly questioned the previous government's delivery on election promises.Pilot called Pargat a "unifying captain", saying the new president has reached out to state leaders and received public support. He has also invoked the team metaphor to describe Congress's approach to the election."You are one captain who's got a fantastic team, and the captain is only as strong as his team," Pilot said he had told Pargat. His appointment, replacing Warring as state chief, was particularly important in the backdrop of an internal tussle between Warring and Channi camps.Punjab Congress has spent months grappling with a bitter power struggle between the camps of state chief Amarinder Singh Raja Warring and former CM Charanjit Singh Channi. The feud spilled into public view through rival sloganeering, poster wars, clashes at party events and boycotts during visits by then state in-charge Bhupesh Baghel. The high command's July compromise, retaining Warring while appointing Channi to head the campaign committee, failed to end the friction. After Sachin Pilot replaced Baghel as Punjab in-charge in September, Warring eventually resigned on October 2, and Pargat Singh was appointed the new state chief.With the Congress leadership now sending the open-door signal to Captain Amarinder, the question is how Pargat's team would accommodate a strong-headed former CM with a history in the party.Moreover, the issue is not limited to Amarinder Singh. In the upcoming months, Congress must also manage the transition from Warring, who led the state unit from April 2022 until October 2026.Congress has also decided against projecting a CM face for the 2027 Punjab election.Pilot said the party would fight as a team and decide who should lead the state after securing the mandate, following consultations with workers, leaders and MLAs."We are fighting together as a team. Let the team win. And then we'll decide who gets to do what job," he said.The party has several experienced leaders, including Partap Singh Bajwa, Sukhjinder Randhawa, Charanjit Singh Channi and Warring. Pargat's appointment adds a new organisational chief to that mix, while the question of Amarinder's possible return remains unconfirmed.For the high command, the practical issue would be defining the role of each leader without undermining the other.Amarinder Singh's long tenure in Punjab politics, his experience as CM and his association with national security and border-state issues are part of his public political profile. A return could give Congress another experienced voice in its campaign, while his criticism of the BJP could offer a new line of political debate. The Congress may gain from his name, polularity and political history but it is unlikely that he would have any active role owing to his age.But the political costs would depend on the terms of any return. His 2021 exit followed a major leadership confrontation, and Pargat was part of the state leadership aligned with Sidhu during that period. Reconciliation would therefore involve not just Amarinder Singh and the Gandhi family, but a state unit whose leadership has changed since he left.It would also raise questions about the position of leaders who remained with Congress through the subsequent elections and organisational changes. Warring's emphasis on youth representation, Pargat's task of consolidating the state unit and Pilot's insistence on collective leadership all point to issues that would need to be addressed.For now, there is no confirmed proposal to bring Captain Amarinder back, no announced role for him and no indication that talks have taken place or are under way.Pilot's "anything is possible" may keep the question open, but the party's immediate task remains to get the current team working together before Punjab votes in 2027.
Article Summary: Sachin Pilot has left the door open to Captain Amarinder Singh's possible return to the Congress. The former Punjab chief minister left Congress in September 2021 after a bitter confrontation with the party's state leadership. Can Congress accommodate its old captain without unsettling the new captain and the team? Where would he fit in a state unit that has just changed leadership and is yet to name a CM face?

Article Title: SC judges jokingly threaten to sit on dharna for foot overbridge and pedestrian path
Article Text:
SC judges jokingly threaten dharna over foot overbridge, pedestrian path

NEW DELHI: In the season of dharnas and protests in Delhi, a Supreme Court bench led by Justice J B Pardiwala last week threatened in a lighter vein to sit on dharna at the Delhi HC main gate if by Nov 25 the govt failed to construct a foot overbridge and pedestrian paths to facilitate safe road crossing for lawyers, litigants and public.Justices Pardiwala and K V Viswanathan told additional solicitor general Vikramjit Banerjee - “If you don't do it before the next date, both of us will be at the main gate of the HC, and we will not go home until you complete the work. That's for sure. Baith jaayenge wahan dharna karne ke liye.”The case related to the stretch of Mathura Road near the HC and Zoological Park, where absence of a foot overbridge and pedestrian safe crossings had been flagged months ago by the SC. Amicus curiae Gaurav Agrawal informed the court on Friday that a traffic signal has been installed. But that did not satisfy the court which threatened sit-in dharna by the judges.If to get a work done for benefit of public, the SC judges, even in lighter vein, feel that dharna is a better option than issuing a mandamus to the govt, then it could have serious implications given the stark contrast between right to expeditious justice and the pendency of more than 95,000 cases in the SC.This is the view expressed by a cross-section of lawyers in lighter vein when TOI sought their responses to Justice Pardiwala's banter.Even if one can tell litigants that they must not complain about the 36,000 cases which are pending 'only' for five years in the apex court which has time and again ruled that right to speedy justice is part of right to life, what would the SC tell the litigants who are waiting patiently for the balance of nearly 60,000 cases?If they decide to enforce their right to speedy justice through dharna at the SC, it would create a law and order situation, which an already stretched Delhi police will find it difficult to handle, the lawyers feared.What about those litigants in the HCs who have been awaiting a hearing in their cases for years together, without expecting a decision? They have been routinely told by the SC to await their chance in the HC and declined then out of turn hearing. maximum such application for a direction for early hearing pertain to the Allahabad HC, where over 12 lakh cases are pending, many for decades. If lakhs of litigants decide to hold dharnas at the HC and its bench at Lucknow, would the police be able to handle the surge of protesters?In the trial courts, the pendency is more than 5.1 crore cases, of which 47 lakh are more than 10 years old and 81 lakh are between 5-10 years-old. What if these litigants, who while awaiting justice have been drained of their finances, are physically exhausted by repeated adjournments and mentally disturbed by the pendency, decide to hold sit-in dharnas at the trial courts?
Article Summary: Justices Pardiwala and K V Viswanathan told additional solicitor general Vikramjit Banerjee - “If you don't do it before the next date, both of us will be at the main gate of the HC, and we will not go home until you complete the work. That's for sure”

Article Title: Young innovators impress juries with ideas to solve real-world challenges
Article Text:
Jury members evaluate entries for TOI’s Ideas for India contest in Delhi

-

Ideas For India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Three separate juries evaluated entries in the three categories for the award and the panel members acknowledged at the end of the day that the quality of applicants was excellent. In each of the categories, bulk of those shortlisted for evaluation by the jury were very young, either still in college or just out of it, though there were some older innovators too.Over 14,000 applications were received, which were filtered down by Techgig to 1,000 and Grant Thornton shortlisted it to 35 finalists that were split between three juries. While first was on sovereign technology for India handled 14 entries, second on Inclusive Innovation for Bharat met a dozen applications and third on Sustainable & Resilient India dealt with nine entries.The juries followed a pattern of a short presentation by the applicants, followed by questions from jury members and then a brief discussion between the members before scoring the applicant. Several jury members admitted that they were pleasantly surprised by how well thought through the presentations were, especially given the age of most applicants.Even where some aspect of the road to implementation may have not occurred to the applicants — say, a compliance issue or consent to be obtained — it was striking how eager the innovators were to learn from the experience of those who had worked in the real world for decades and knew what it takes to translate brilliant ideas into real solutions.The maturity to take hard questions as essential inputs rather than as harsh criticism was quite remarkable.The diversity of the presentations was also a striking aspect. In the technology sovereignty category, for instance, the ideas ranged from closing a felt gap in middle sized drones to faster and more efficient identification and countering of cyberattacks to dealing with ships that go ‘dark’, which may not always be for innocent reasons.But these were not just ideas. The drone entry had already done some testing in the field with army units, the dark ships idea had been explored with a port and so on.Such was the overall quality of the applicants that at least in two categories some of the jury members voiced the opinion that perhaps the awards need not be restricted to two in each category. There was, after all, no compulsion to stick to a bell curve, they pointed out. Most left the venue feeling satisfied that they had done their bit to encourage a cohort whose innovative mindset was matched by its enthusiasm to do good for society and for India.
Article Summary: Over 14,000 applications were received, which were filtered down by Techgig to 1,000 and Grant Thornton shortlisted it to 35 finalists that were split between three juries. Jury members admitted that they were pleasantly surprised by how well thought through the presentations were, especially given the age of most applicants.

Article Title: Amit Shah to pay tribute to police martyrs, launch nationwide anti-drug rally on October 21
Article Text:
Union home minister Amit Shah will pay homage to the police martyrs by laying a wreath at the memorial, besides addressing the event.

NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah will on Wednesday mark the Police Commemoration Day, observed on October 21 every year, by paying homage to the police martyrs at the National Police Memorial.He will also flag off a motorcycle rally of about 90 police riders from Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh and Delhi)Central Armed Police Forces (CRPF, CISF, BSF, SSB, ITBP and NSG) and some Central Police Organisations (RPF, NDRF and NIA). This is part of a nationwide rally themed on ‘Fight Against Drugs’, wherein police riders from all states/UTs and Central Forces would reach Ekta Nagar, Gujarat to join the Ekta Parade on Octoberober 31, 2026.The Police Commemoration Day is celebrated in honour of ten valiant policemen who laid down their lives on October 21, 1959, in an ambush laid by heavily armed Chinese troops at Hot Springs, Ladakh. In recognition of the sacrifices made by police personnel and their paramount role in preserving national security and integrity, the Prime Minister dedicated the National Police Memorial (NPM), Chanakyapuri, New Delhi to the nation on Police Commemoration Day 2018.On October 21, an event will be organised at the National Police Memorial, New Delhi, where a joint parade of Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) and Delhi Police would be held. The home minister will preside over the function, to be attended by retired DGs, officers from the police fraternity and other dignitaries.Shah will pay homage to the police martyrs by laying a wreath at the memorial, besides addressing the event.As part of the remembrances, CAPFs/CPOs will organise various commemorative events at NPM from October 22 to 30, which will include visits of family members of martyrs, police band display, motorcycle rallies, Run for Martyrs, blood donation camps, essay/painting competitions for children and display of video films showcasing sacrifice, valour and services of police personnel. Similar programmes will be organised simultaneously by all the police Forces across the country.

Union home minister Amit Shah will pay homage to the police martyrs by laying a wreath at the memorial, besides addressing the event.

Article Title: Around 1575, a Mughal artist painted a cheetah family on cloth during Akbar's reign; about 450 years later, the tiny work from Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan's collection sold for nearly Rs 120 crore in Lo

What’s so interesting about the painting

Who was Basawan?

When art became a record

From a royal-era painting to a private collection

How a painting estimated at ₹8 crore sold for nearly ₹120 crore

Not all paintings in the world are being sold in crores. But there’s one particular painting titled A Family of Cheetahs in a Rocky Landscape that was sold for nearly Rs 120 crore in London. It created a stir in the world of painting and made headlines. This is the painting attributed to Basawan, one of the most prominent painters associated with Akbar’s court.Back in 1575–80, when Mughal emperor Akbar was building one of the most influential courts in Indian history, Basawan created an extraordinary painting of a family of cheetahs. The painting which was made nearly 450 years ago has survived and has seen several empires rise and fall. It witnessed the ever-changing artistic tastes and centuries of collecting.In October 2025, the painting made headlines when it was sold at Christie’s in London for £10.245 million (₹119 crore at the time).If you look at the painting, it doesn’t look like a grand royal portrait. The painting’s beauty lies in its remarkably detailed study of animals in their natural surroundings.Yet this intimate glimpse into the wildlife of Mughal India became one of the most valuable paintings of its kind ever sold at auction.According to Christie’s, the sale also set a world auction record for a Classical Indian or Islamic painting. What makes the story particularly fascinating is that the artwork’s importance extends far beyond its extraordinary price, offering a glimpse into the artistic imagination. It shows the royal interests of sixteenth-century India.The painting belongs to a flourishing period of Mughal art. Akbar was an artist who supported a flourishing royal workshop where Indian and Persian artistic traditions came together. Painters working under imperial patronage developed a distinctive style and created masterpieces worth remembering.Basawan was a leading artist from the Akbar period. His work is largely associated with innovation and expressive figures. The cheetah painting, dated to approximately 1575–80, is attributed to him rather than being definitively signed by the artist.What makes this painting unique is its subject. Rather than depicting any royal figure or a scene from a religious book, it focuses on animals in their natural habitat. The composition brings together art and observation.The Mughal fascination with animals was not just decorative. Hunting, falconry and the keeping of exotic animals were part of courtly life. Akbar and other Mughal emperors maintained elaborate courts in which artists recorded people, events, landscapes, plants and animals. Under Akbar’s successor Jahangir, naturalistic painting became prominent, with artists producing remarkably detailed studies of birds and animals.Against this background, a family of cheetahs is an evocative subject. The painting does not simply use an animal as a symbol of royal power; it presents a glimpse of wildlife as a subject worthy of close artistic attention.The artwork went on to become part of the personal collection of Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan and Princess Catherine Aga Khan. Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan (1933–2003) was a diplomat and philanthropist who served as the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees from 1965 to 1977. He was also a collector of unique artwork. The couple acquired much of their collection between the 1960s and the 1980s. Many of the paintings they selected were later studied and published by scholars. They were also put you display.The collection was displayed at Château de Bellerive, their home on the shores of Lake Geneva in Switzerland. The cheetah painting was among 95 works offered at Christie’s London auction on October 28, 2025.Before the auction, Christie’s estimated the cheetah painting at £700,000 to £1 million. Its eventual sale price of £10,245,000, including the buyer’s premium, was approximately 14 times more than its estimate.The result was also the highlight of the wider auction, which totalled £45.76 million, six times its pre-sale estimate. Every lot sold, with bidders registered across 20 countries and four continents, according to Christie’s.
Article Summary: A Family of Cheetahs in a Rocky Landscape, attributed to Basawan, Mughal India, circa 1575-80, sold at Christie’s in London for £10.245 million in October 2025. The painting is one of the most valuable paintings of its kind ever sold at auction. The sale also set a world auction record for a Classical Indian or Islamic painting.

Article Title: ‘India is not Bangladesh or France’: Tharoor hits back at BJP, says opposition backs peaceful protest
Article Text:
‘We believe in peaceful protest’: Tharoor rejects BJP’s India-Bangladesh comparison

Political row over ‘regime change’

Tharoor comments on Musk's Starlink remarks

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor on Monday rejected comparisons between India and Bangladesh or France amid the political row over the opposition's use of the phrase “regime change”, asserting that the demand was for free and fair elections and not an attempt to topple the government.Responding to Union minister Kiren Rijiju's remarks, Tharoor said India did not support violence and that protests should remain peaceful. He also questioned the relevance of comparisons with unrest in other countries."I think that India is not Bangladesh and India is not France. I don't see these analogies as particularly relevant... We would never condone any of the violence, setting alight buses and police stations and so on, that has occurred in France. We only believe in peaceful protest... that's the kind of protest that I have participated in, and that I believe the opposition in general supports... As far as the larger issues are concerned, there's no point distorting a phrase like 'regime change' and so on. .. What we are calling for is free and fair elections... What is troubling today is that large numbers of people have been cut from the electoral rolls as the result of a completely troublesome, irregular, and partially illegal process.This is why we are calling for all this to be undone... It's a constitutional issue. It's not an issue of trying to topple a regime or anything like that..."Tharoor also defended citizens' right to protect democratic institutions, while clarifying that his criticism was directed at their functioning and not their existence."...Democracy is not a gift of anybody... we, the ordinary citizens of India, are the custodians of it... Every Indian citizen has the right to protect our democracy... All I'm saying is we are asking institutions like the Election Commission to behave themselves, to perform as they are required to by the democratic Constitution of India. That's all it is. I'm not in any way challenging these institutions as institutions. I'm challenging the way they are behaving, the way they are conducting themselves, and that is something that honestly all of us in India should be concerned about..."The remarks came amid a political exchange over protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and allegations of irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.On Sunday, Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju alleged that “anti-India groups” and some politicians had colluded to provoke young people and spread violence, claiming that a conspiracy similar to the unrest in Bangladesh and France had been planned in India.“The violent incident that occurred in Bangladesh and the riots, arson, and looting that took place in France, a similar conspiracy was hatched for India as well,” Rijiju said in a post on X.He further asserted that a change of government in India could take place only through elections.“Regime change in India is absolutely possible, but only through elections, not through Soros,” he said.The row intensified after senior advocate Prashant Bhushan described the agitation against Kumar as a “fight for regime change”. All India Students' Association (AISA) president Neha Bora also referred to the Gen Z-led movement in Bangladesh.Rijiju had earlier accused political rivals and activists of using street protests to create unrest and destabilise constitutional institutions. He said India's youth were focused on nation-building rather than political upheaval.Separately, Tharoor responded to Elon Musk's recent remarks regarding Starlink, saying the government had maintained that all companies bidding for the service were going through the same process and facing similar delays."I've heard the government's explanation on this issue, which is that there is a process and that all the companies bidding for this are in the same process and are facing the same delays. If that position of the government is taken literally, that means Musk is no further behind in the queue, and Ambani is no further ahead. I think we just have to wait for the process to play itself out... There are several factors. There are questions of the technology, certain security concerns, various kinds of details to do with the uplinking and finally cost.The last one, the ordinary public will decide. If you are giving me a service and he's giving it to me for 10 times the price, I may take it from you. Or if I really feel that what he's doing is worth 10 times the money, I'll give it to him. Each subscriber will have to decide. Personally, I'm quite happy with my regular connections. I'm not looking for a Starlink myself. But if there are people who feel these things are useful, in a free country, let them have the opportunity."
Article Summary: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor rejects comparisons between India and Bangladesh or France. He says India does not support violence and that protests should remain peaceful. The remarks came amid a political exchange over protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and allegations of irregularities.

Article Title: 6 in 10 men over 45 unaware of their prostate cancer screening status: Survey
Article Text:

NEW DELHI:

Nearly six in 10 Indian men aged 45 and above do not know whether they have ever been screened for prostate cancer, while only around one in six report having undergone screening, a survey by NGO Heal Foundation has found.The survey of 1,036 men across Delhi-NCR, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana and Maharashtra points to significant gaps in awareness of prostate cancer risk factors, screening and when to seek medical advice. Nearly 69% of respondents could not name a single risk factor, while only 13.2% recognised family history as one. Around three-fourths believed prostate cancer monitoring should begin only at age 50 or later.The findings highlight a disconnect between routine healthcare and prostate-specific awareness. Although 62% of respondents said they underwent annual health check-ups, 60.8% did not know their prostate cancer screening status and only about 16% reported having ever been screened.Awareness of the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test was also limited. Only around 31% had heard of PSA as a marker, and just 14% had specifically requested the test.“These findings point to a fundamental awareness gap around prostate cancer,” said Dr Devavrat Arya, vice-chairman, medical oncology, Max Healthcare, Delhi. He said awareness of risk factors, screening and when to consult a doctor needed to become a more visible part of routine health conversations among men over 45.The survey found that 59.5% of men were uncomfortable discussing screening or treatment with doctors, while only 18% would initiate the conversation themselves. Although 67% trusted doctors and hospitals, just 36% identified a urologist as the appropriate specialist. Meanwhile, 84% searched online or on social media for health information.The biggest barriers to screening were believing it was unnecessary (34%), having no symptoms (28%) and not receiving a doctor's recommendation (22%). Cost (19%), embarrassment or privacy concerns (17%), fear of diagnosis (14%) and not knowing where to go (11%) were other reasons.Gaps widened with age: around 72% of men aged 65 and above were unsure of their screening status, while 80% reported low treatment knowledge. Overall, 71.2% had limited knowledge of treatment options, only 10% felt confident across the treatment pathway, and 44% wanted a second opinion before treatment.Dr Nitesh Rohatgi, principal director of medical oncology at fortis memorial research institute, said symptoms in older men were often dismissed as ageing, delaying diagnosis, while awareness of advanced treatments such as radioligand therapy remained limited even after diagnosis.The findings highlight the need for greater risk awareness and informed discussions with doctors. However, the survey reflects self-reported awareness and screening experiences, not prostate cancer prevalence or screening rates among all Indian men.
Article Summary: Survey of 1,036 men across Delhi-NCR, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana and Maharashtra points to significant gaps in awareness of prostate cancer risk factors, screening and when to seek medical advice. Nearly 69% of respondents could not name a single risk factor, while only 13.2% recognised family history as one.

Article Title: Is college worth it in 2026
Article Text:

In our twenties, when there is still so much time ahead of us, time that seems ample for a hundred indecisions, for a hundred visions and revisions—we draw a card, and we must decide right then and there whether to keep that card and discard the next, or discard the first card and keep the second. And before we know it, the deck has been played out and the decisions we have just made will shape our lives for decades to come. Rules of Civility, Amor Towles

On self-learning

Why do we go to university?

A Bend in the River

opportunity of discovering yourself

Schooling may not only affect income but also the degree to which one enjoys working or the likelihood of not being able to find work. Schooling could also lead individuals to make better decisions about health, marriage, and parenting style. It may have significant consumption value too. And, as we argue in this paper, schooling may affect preferences in a way that makes individuals more patient, more goal-oriented, and less likely to engage in risky behavior. In short, schooling may have important nonpecuniary returns. — Philip Oreopoulos and Kjell G. Salvanes, “Priceless: The Nonpecuniary Benefits of Schooling”

Again, you can’t connect the dots looking forward. You can only connect them looking backwards, so you have to trust that the dots will somehow connect in your future.

The pay gap between having a university degree and not having one

-

Many years ago, I went to my parents expressing my wish to drop a year to prepare for IIT-JEE. It was a particularly stressful time for us financially, and yet, my parents did not think twice before fully supporting me in this risky endeavour. As grateful as I am to my parents, I am probably not unique. As I entered IIT Kharagpur the following year, I met several others who came through very humble backgrounds, students whose parents had pledged their land, or taken an extra job or a loan to provide the best opportunities to their children. For most parents, the choice was self-evident. A good undergraduate degree was a way to move up the social ladder.But lately, people have started questioning the worth of a university education. They contend that the university model is outdated today due to rapid technological advancements. In particular, given that we can now learn everything online using AI, we do not need a university degree. And in any case, the pay gap between those with a degree and those without no longer justifies the ever-rising costs.This view is wrong on three counts. First, it overstates the challenge that awaits us because it ignores the harsh reality of people’s ability to learn on their own.Second, it misses what learning at a university entails. And finally, the pay gap it disputes is still very much there.First, questions like whether our existing methods of teaching, working, and thinking are suited to the looming changes are hardly new. When computers arrived, apocalyptic prophecies about employment prospects were ubiquitous. Those arguing that the knowledge from a university degree is redundant over a person’s career miss the point that this is how it has always been. A person graduating in 1980 would have barely seen a computer. In 2005, they might not have known how to work without one. A person graduating in 1990 in India would most likely not have known what an email was; in 2020, their entire workflow would have been online. It is tempting to think this time is different. But, as they say, the more things change, the more they stay the same. A good university education teaches us how to learn and not what to learn. Neither AI nor most jobs will teach that.And what is the historical track record of self-learning? Top scholars from the world’s best universities like Stanford and MIT have made knowledge freely available for nearly two decades now. Gilbert Strang, one of the giants of linear algebra (the field that is at the heart of machine learning and AI), has a course on Linear Algebra on YouTube . The first lecture has 4.9 million views. By the last lecture, we have about 200K-250K views. A macroeconomics course drops from 860K to 15K, a deep learning course drops from 518K to 4.7K, you get the drift. In short, the fraction of people who manage to complete a course delivered by some of the best scholars in the world is anywhere from 1 in 20 to 1 in 100. After all, self-discipline and the art of learning have to be acquired. Universities allow the students to learn them the hard way by failing, struggling, and catching up. If being an Eklavya was so easy, Eklavya would not have made it into history in the first place!Recent evidence makes this concrete. David Strömberg and his co-authors tracked some 27,000 Chinese schoolchildren aged 12 to 18, roughly 80% of whom had taken to using models like DeepSeek. Within six months their homework scores had risen by 18%, and the time spent on each assignment had fallen from 64 minutes to 45. So far so good. But at exam time, those same pupils scored 20% below classmates who had never used AI. Most telling of all, the old relationship inverted: homework scores used to predict exam performance, and now the pupils with the best homework are the likeliest to stumble in the exam. A randomised experiment in Turkish classrooms points to the remedy—the damage largely disappears when the AI is set up to give teacher-designed hints rather than answers. In short, the irresistible temptation to fetch an answer immediately—much like scrolling reels to kill time—sounds the death knell of learning. Since much of the payoff in the labour market lies precisely in the harder skills, the relevance of the university is likely to persist.There is another challenge with self-learning. Most academics at good universities have far better information about their students than any online platform and can and do design courses that are better suited to their tastes, abilities, and contexts. For example, at ISB, a course on antitrust policies covers a range of cases from the US and India; a course on Indian National Financial Systems goes deep into the Indian economy through the lens of cutting-edge research in economics. I am yet to come across a place outside the university system where one can learn the foundational principles of these topics without wasting hours on obscure and irrelevant material.Second, there is a fundamental question: Does one attend a university only to be taught by professors? Here, I cannot do better than ancient Sanskrit wisdom.आचार्यात्पादमादत्ते पादं शिष्यः स्वमेधया। पादं सब्रह्मचारिभ्यः पादं कालक्रमेण च॥You learn a quarter from the teacher, a quarter through your own intellect, a quarter through fellow classmates, and a quarter from the passage of time. The internet at its best replaces only the teacher’s quarter—and even that I doubt; the other three quarters are what the campus is for. If one switches to a self-learning model, would it be so easy to find fellow classmates who are driven by shared interests, passions, and energy to learn?VS Naipaul once wrote, in, “we make ourselves according to the ideas we have of our possibilities.” A good university reveals to us our possibilities, our challenges and limitations; it exposes us to people better than us and opens our horizons to the opportunities that await us. Skipping university education comes at the cost of denying yourself the opportunity to learn seemingly unrelated and unimportant subjects, the opportunity to engage in intellectually stimulating conversations with your classmates, and above all, the. The unstructured time, the enduring friendships and debates, transform us from adolescents to adults, to people. As Oreopoulos and Salvanes show Schooling creates adults of the kind we need; the robots who’d maximise productivity can be provided by technology.The obsession with finding the “use case” for every course, every lecture, is rather counterproductive. As Steve Jobs, the patron saint of dropping out, said in his famous Stanford commencement speech:And finally, even if one accepts all these benefits, are the costs—time lost and the tuition paid—worth it? Do graduates get paid significantly more? To slightly paraphrase the apocryphal quote of Mark Twain, the reports of the death of the college premium—the additional salaries that college graduates receive relative to their non-college peers—are greatly exaggerated. For example, in a recent article in the Financial Times , John Burn-Murdoch highlighted how the hourly wage premium for university graduates in the US has begun to slip: from a peak of roughly 85% to below 80% today. Unfortunately, such statistics are not available for India, so we must base the arguments mostly on estimates from the West.Focusing on the decline, though, risks losing the bigger picture: a university education still pays a significant premium, and is likely to keep doing so.Still, I must concede one point. The perception that university education has stopped being useful is shaped by recent studies showing rising graduate unemployment in the US and a collapsing graduate job market in the UK . Over the past few decades, as the belief about the “college-premium” got cemented, universities floated several “soft” undergraduate programmes to earn quick money. It is no surprise that people graduating from such degrees would eventually struggle in the labour market. The median early-career salary (ages 22–27) of computer science graduates in the US is $87,000 ( NY Fed data ), while it can be as low as $43,000 for some other disciplines. Indeed, the falling average premium may say less about the democratisation of technical knowledge than about the rapid rise of degrees whose worth the labour market is yet to discover. Several empirical studies establish that even taking the costs into account, most undergraduate education in rigorous fields pays off heavily . The problem is not university education; it is the choice of discipline!Echoing Towles’ protagonist in the opening quote, it may be seductive to embrace a paradigm shift after listening to the confident predictions about the demise of the university model. But it would be rather foolish to play the deck of one’s life, to make choices that will shape your life for decades to come, listening to confident projections about a very uncertain world. It is natural to feel encumbered by the gravity of looming changes in the world that awaits us. We must take comfort in the fact that people have always felt it, in 1960, 1980, 2000, and today. As I was graduating, my PhD advisor David Pearce from New York University gave me a piece of advice that has remained the mantra of my life. One evening in his office, discussing my plans for the years ahead, David said, “Aditya, just take care of the pennies, and the pounds will take care of themselves.” The chances are, if I had not gone to a university, I wouldn’t have learned this, let alone practised it. This was not a part of any curriculum. And that is the beauty of university education: the chance interactions that shape our lives are likely to remain important as long as humans continue to teach humans.
Article Summary: Schooling may not only affect income but also the degree to which one enjoys working or the likelihood of not being able to find work. Schooling could also lead individuals to make better decisions about health, marriage, and parenting style. The pay gap between having a university degree and not having one is still very much there.

NEW DELHI: A 44-year-old woman, just 98 cm tall and weighing 22 kg, has undergone laparoscopic hysterectomy at AIIMS , with doctors adapting the surgical approach to minimise fracture risks from severe osteoporosis and address anaesthesia challenges linked to her exceptionally small stature.The woman, who has been living with osteoporosis, or fragile bones, since 2019, had suffered from extremely painful menstrual periods for nearly a year. The pain disrupted her daily life, forcing her to rely frequently on painkillers. Investigations revealed deep pelvic endometriosis and adenomyosis, a condition in which tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus or within its muscular wall.Prof Neena Malhotra, head of Obstetrics and gynaecology said that the patient recovered well and was discharged on the third day after surgery.Given her age, bone fragility and high blood pressure, hormonal treatment was not considered feasible.Doctors recommended removing the uterus to relieve her symptoms. Teams from gynaecology, endocrinology and anaesthesia jointly assessed the risks before proceeding with minimally invasive surgery.“Minimally invasive surgery is now routine for most hysterectomies, but operating on an adult woman of this size, with severe bone weakness and hypertension, poses unusual challenges,” said Prof K Aparna Sharma from the department of obstetric and gynaecology.A major concern was positioning the patient. The conventional lithotomy position, in which the legs are raised and supported, could have exposed her lower back and thigh bones to fractures.“Due to short stature along with severely fragile bones, standard lithotomy position for hysterectomy could have put her at risk of lower back and thigh bone fractures. There was a need for utmost care in proper positioning and cushioning during surgery,” said Prof Rajesh Khadgawat of the endocrinology department.At the request of the patient and her family, the team opted to perform the procedure with her lying flat on her back, taking precautions to minimise injury.“The uterus was enlarged due to adenomyosis, and the uterus and ovaries were stuck to the adjacent intestines, while the space in her abdomen was very limited. We were able to complete the hysterectomy successfully through the laparoscopic route in around 90 minutes,” said Prof Reeta Mahey, who performed the surgery.
Article Summary: The woman, who has been living with osteoporosis, or fragile bones, since 2019, had suffered from extremely painful menstrual periods for nearly a year. Investigations revealed deep pelvic endometriosis and adenomyosis, a condition in which tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus or within its muscular wall.

Article Title: IMD launches WebGIS-based decision support system to improve cyclone disaster preparedness
Article Text:
The India Meteorological Department has launched an advanced WebGIS platform designed to boost disaster preparedness against cyclones.

NEW DELHI: As an additional disaster preparedness tool to support ground-level action ahead of cyclones, India meteorological department (IMD) has launched an interactive WebGIS-based platform that will serve as a decision support system (DSS), bringing critical cyclone warnings and marine weather information together in one place.The system will help users, including disaster management authorities, govt agencies and the general public, better understand potential hazards and their likely impacts. It aims to bridge the gap between weather forecasts and their practical application, enabling better preparedness, timely action and enhanced public safety during cyclones and other severe weather events.The launch took place during the bi-annual pre-cyclone exercise meeting for the post-monsoon season (Oct-Dec) under the chairmanship of Mrutyunjay Mohapatra, director general of meteorology, IMD, last week. The DSS platform for the public isavailable on the websites of IMD and regional specialised meteorological centre (RSMC).“Through interactive maps and visualisations of cyclone tracks, intensity, winds, rainfall, storm surge and rainfall forecasts for river catchments, the platform helps users access relevant information and make informed decisions,” said the ministry of earth sciences (MoES) in a statement.IMD has taken a number of steps in recent years to continuously enhance the capabilities in monitoring, numerical modelling and forecasting of the hazards associated with cyclones, and demonstrated its capability to provide early warning for cyclones with high precision. It has, over the years, emerged as the best in the world for the accuracy of cyclone predictions, reporting zero error on the landfall point and timing.A cyclone is an intense vortex or a whirl in the atmosphere with very strong winds circulating around it in an anti-clockwise direction in the Northern Hemisphere and in a clockwise direction in the Southern hemisphere. The word "Cyclone" is derived from the greek word “Cyclos" meaning the coil of a snake. Tropical cyclones are also referred to as 'Hurricanes' over Atlantic Ocean, 'Typhoons' over Pacific Ocean, 'Willy-Willies' over Australian Seas and simply as 'Cyclones' over north Indian ocean.On an average, out of five cyclones developing over the north Indian ocean (NIO) comprising bay of Bengal and Arabian sea annually, about three to four of them make landfall causing loss of life and property. Low - lying coastal belts of West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry are more prone to the impact of these systems.The number of deaths due to cyclones has, however, decreased significantly in the recent past, as a result of the improvement in the early warning capabilities of IMD.
Article Summary: The system will help users, including disaster management authorities, govt agencies and the general public, better understand potential hazards and their likely impacts. The launch took place during the bi-annual pre-cyclone exercise meeting for the post-monsoon season.

Article Title: Presidential election today? Trump confuses India with Brazil, claims 125 million voted

Trump says "125 million Indians voted in presidential election today."

US President Donald Trump on Monday confused India with Brazil, claiming that 125 million people had voted in an Indian “presidential election”, while also questioning the integrity of the American voting system.In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote, “125 Million People voted today in the first round of India’s Presidential Election. The results came out shortly after the vote closed, on the same day!”He then compared the alleged election results with the US electoral process, writing, “In Detroit, Philadelphia, California, and numerous other US Cities and States, the results, with much smaller numbers, will often take weeks to Rig, I mean, calculate. Voting in America is corrupt!!!”However, India did not hold a presidential election on Sunday. The President of India is elected indirectly by an electoral college and not through a direct nationwide popular vote.Trump's remarks came after Brazil held the first round of its presidential election on Sunday, with incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro advancing to the October 25 runoff.With 99.99% of the votes counted, Bolsonaro secured 47.03% of the valid votes, while Lula received 45.16%, according to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court.The figure of around 125 million mentioned by Trump is close to Brazil's total valid votes, which stood at about 125.27 million, suggesting he may have confused the Brazilian election with India.Neither Bolsonaro nor Lula crossed the 50% threshold required to win in the first round, triggering the October 25 runoff, BBC reported.Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, outperformed expectations in the first round and finished ahead of Lula. His strong showing has raised the prospect of a shift to the right in Latin America's largest economy.Brazil has used electronic voting for decades, and electoral authorities said the first-round voting process proceeded smoothly.The Organization of American States' electoral observation mission said “the voting has been going smoothly and under adequate safety conditions.”The rapid announcement of results has also been cited as a strength of Brazil's electronic voting system.“When results take a lot of time, it creates an opening for people to cast doubt on the results, to say there’s been a problem,” Josemar Lauriano Pereira, a 46-year-old lawyer in Rio de Janeiro, told the Associated Press.Trump's post drew reactions on social media, with users pointing out that India does not elect its president through a direct popular vote.One user posted, “Trump living in a different world? Is a presidential election taking place in India? President Donald Trump made the incorrect claim that 125 million people voted in India's "presidential election" today.”Another said, “What is my blud Donald Trump smoking? Why is he mentioning India instead of Brazil when talking about the election?”
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump confused India with Brazil, claiming that 125 million people had voted in an Indian "presidential election" He also questioned the integrity of the American voting system. India did not hold a presidential election on Sunday. The President of India is elected indirectly by an electoral college.

Article Title: SIR strikes at heart of Constitution: Supreme Court judge Ujjal Bhuyan
Article Text:
File photo: Supreme Court of India Judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan (PTI Photo)

Detaching right to vote from citizen is like taking soul out of body: Bhuyan

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Launching a scathing attack on special intensive revision (SIR) that has resulted in large-scale deletion of names from voter lists across states, Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan on Sunday said any process disenfranchising millions of Indian citizens was intrinsically arbitrary as it struck at the heart of the Constitution.Discounting the reasons given by govt and EC to justify SIR, which was upheld in the case of the revision of rolls in West Bengal by SC with modifications, Justice Bhuyan said, "No amount of whataboutery can justify it. It strikes at the very heart of Constitution. I would go to the extent of saying that it is a negation of the constitutional order which we have adopted under the Constitution."He was speaking at the moot court valedictory function at Nalsar, Hyderabad.Nalsar students, who had opposed CJI Surya Kant's participation in the convocation ceremony recently, came in for praise from Justice Bhuyan.Also read| Democracy in peril as voters illegally ousted: Former SC judge Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman "One last word about the brilliant students of Nalsar. You have shown to the country and to the world what a university student, that too a student of law, should be. You are brilliant, you are bold, and you are brave," he said.Justice Bhuyan said a citizen’s right to vote was central to the holding of free and fair elections.“Except in the case of a dead voter, the name of a voter once enlisted in the electoral roll cannot be deleted without notice and hearing,” he added.The SC judge said the right to vote or be included in the voters’ list could not be detached from the persona of an Indian citizen.Also read: EC orders special drive to add genuine electors 'left out' during SIR “If it is done, it will be like taking out the soul from the body,” he added. Justice Bhuyan said the Indian Constitution does not provide for two classes of citizens: citizens with voting rights and citizens without voting rights. “Any process which leads to wholesale disenfranchisement of Indian citizens, making them citizens without voting rights, would be violative of Articles 326 and 14 of Constitution of India,” he said.“If any process results in disenfranchising millions and millions of Indian citizens, making them second class citizens in their own country in the sense of being citizens without voting rights, such a process is intrinsically arbitrary,” he added, his remarks coinciding with attacks on EC and govt over SIR by the opposition and others.Justice Bhuyan said the right to vote was intertwined with India’s years of struggle against foreign rule. “It is a manifestation of our freedom achieved after so much struggle and sacrifice. Article 326 (universal adult franchise) cannot be tinkered with at all. No authority can do it, no court can condone it. No one is above Constitution,” he said.
Article Summary: Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan said any process disenfranchising millions of Indian citizens was intrinsically arbitrary as it struck at the heart of the Constitution. He was speaking at the moot court valedictory function at Nalsar, Hyderabad. “If it is done, it will be like taking out the soul from the body,” he added.

Aaron Rodgers’ parents, Ed and Darla Rodgers, sold their longtime California property for $1.68 million. They secured a significant profit on the property they purchased almost two decades ago.As per Realtor, Ed and Darla Rodgers’ five-bedroom mansion in Chico, California, was sold just weeks after being listed on the market. They initially listed the mansion for $1.75 million but eventually sold it for $1.68 million, still a significant increase over its purchase price.The Rodgers family sold their property just as Aaron was navigating another season with the Pittsburgh Steelers in May 2026. Their son, too, has his own Wisconsin mansion on the market.Aaron Rodgers’ parents, Ed and Darla Rodgers, purchased the California property in 2007 for $306,000. The mansion was bought two years after Rodgers was drafted by the Green Bay Packers. The 5,300-square-foot residence boasts a Victorian Craftsman style and sits on over 3 acres.Among its features are smart home technology, a custom theater room, a separate one-bedroom apartment, a 3-car garage, and a hot tub.According to the property’s listing, the residence boasts timeless finishes, indoor-outdoor living spaces, and thoughtfully designed areas that offer the family living there - the comfort of a home.Rodgers spent his childhood with his siblings in Chico. His father played football for the Chico State Wildcats. Aaron attended Pleasant Valley High School. He played college football for the California Golden Bears. By the time Rodgers’ parents purchased the Chico property, he had already left for the NFL.Aaron Rodgers’ parents’ California mansion was sold, but his own Wisconsin mansion still remains on the market. The Hobart mansion was listed for $3.7 million in November 2025.The Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback listed the Wisconsin mansion for $2.8 million in 2024 but withdrew it due to sentimental attachment to the area.Rodgers purchased the massive property for just over $1.7 million in 2015, when he played for the Green Bay Packers. The 10,500 sq-ft property sits on a 5.32-acre lot. Lush greenery and numerous trees surround it, providing desirable privacy.The luxurious abode boasts a billiard room with a bar, a brick theater with built-in seating and a wet bar, a fitness room, a steam shower, a wine cellar, and a changing room. Exteriorly, the mansion features a patio with a fire pit, a greenhouse, and tennis and pickleball courts.In 2016, Aaron Rodgers’ younger brother Jordan Rodgers appeared on The Bachelorette. Jordan spoke about the distance between Aaron and the rest of the family. He expressed sadness over their strained relationship and hoped for reconciliation.In 2017, Aaron’s father, Ed, told The New York Times that Aaron had not spoken to the family since 2014. He hoped that their relationship could improve. In 2024, Aaron spoke about his family in the Netflix documentary, Aaron Rodgers: Enigma.The quarterback said losing his family connection was heartbreaking for him. He largely kept the matter private.Then in July 2026, Aaron posted five snapshots of his beautiful family, parents - Ed and Darla Rodgers and brother Luke, on his Instagram. A user commented on the photos, “his wife definitely made this [family reunion] happen.”Aaron is married to Brittani, whom he met in 2017. “In 2017, I met my wife, and at the time, she was leaving the States and going back to Europe.And my biggest regret is not begging her to stay or proposing right there, because that sent me right there into a tailspin of what I can be accused of as a partner in a relationship,” Aaron told Pittsburgh teammate Cam Heyward in September 2026.Aaron met his wife Brittani while she was living in Austin, Texas, after attending the University of Texas at Austin. He also credited her with helping him reunite with his family.“A year ago, even two years ago, five years ago for sure, I would have said, ‘Naah, I’m never going to reconcile,’” Aaron said. “My wife deserves a lot of the credit for that just to be able to get to that point to think about having the conversations, she was a big part of that.And not that she was pushing anything; she wasn’t. It was more, and you guys can probably relate to this, when you’re loved by someone in such an unconditional, beautiful, pure way, it changes your perspective on all of your relationships around that; that becomes your anchor point.Well, if I can be made to feel like this by this person, I feel like it opens up your heart in an even deeper way that I never experienced before.”Aaron’s family attended the Week 5 game to cheer him up. This surely feels like his final year. His team, the Pittsburgh Steelers, won against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, 19-26 in Week 6. His team now boasts 4 wins and 2 losses in the 2026 NFL season.

Cristiano Ronaldo's decision to walk out of Portugal's national team camp following a reported disagreement with coach Jorge Jesus has cost the superstar forward a 30-day suspension and a fine of €255 ($285), with the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) describing the punishment as “adequate and sufficient”.The FPF announced the disciplinary decision on Monday, confirming that the 41-year-old had admitted the facts underlying the charges in a formal statement submitted on Friday. His admission and clean disciplinary record were considered mitigating circumstances, helping reduce the sanction. The fine was the maximum permitted after those circumstances were taken into account.Ronaldo, who had already apologised for his actions and acknowledged that he deserved to be punished, can appeal the decision. The Portugal captain had not immediately reacted publicly to the announcement.The controversy erupted during Portugal's recent Nations League campaign after Ronaldo was left on the bench for the team's match against Norway on September 27. Portugal won the game 2-1, but the forward was reportedly frustrated after being left unused despite believing that Jesus had assured him he would feature for around 30 minutes.Ronaldo also accused the coach of breaking a second agreement to publicly explain the situation. Jesus denied making any such promises but left the door open for the forward's return after the match.The disagreement escalated when Ronaldo left Portugal's training camp ahead of the subsequent Nations League fixture against Denmark. The Portuguese Football Federation subsequently initiated disciplinary proceedings over the incident, with the case formally opened in October.The federation's disciplinary council found that Ronaldo had intentionally committed an offence under Article 160(1) of its disciplinary regulations. The player had also apologised for failing to acknowledge supporters after the Norway match and for leaving his teammates, while accepting that his conduct could not go unpunished.Despite the disciplinary action, Ronaldo is expected to be available for Portugal's next Nations League fixture against Denmark on November 14. The suspension began on October 1, the day of the Denmark match, allowing the forward to serve a substantial portion of the 30-day punishment before his anticipated return.Portugal managed to progress in the Nations League without their captain, registering victories over Denmark and Norway after the controversy. The results helped the side secure qualification for the quarter-finals.FPF president Pedro Proenca has also indicated that the federation wants Ronaldo back in the national setup once the matter is resolved.The relatively modest financial penalty is unlikely to be the main consequence for the Al-Nassr forward. Instead, the suspension serves as a disciplinary reminder that even Portugal's most prominent player is subject to the federation's rules, regardless of his standing in the national side.

Article Title: “Spend an hour of your time and give something”: How Tom Brady's high school habit inspired a blood donation drive that drew 20,000 donors and could save 60,000 lives
Article Text:
Tom Brady's high school habit inspired a blood donation drive that drew 20,000 donors and could save 60,000 lives(Image via Getty Images)

Tom Brady reveals the high school habit behind his blood donation campaign

How Tom Brady's Big Ten blood drive raised $1 million for community health

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Tom Brady has spent years chasing records on the football field. But one habit he picked up long before his NFL career has nothing to do with touchdowns or Super Bowl rings. Brady has donated blood since high school. In Sept. 2024, he used that experience to encourage college football fans to do the same, joining a campaign that brought rival schools together for a cause bigger than the game.The former New England Patriots and Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback teamed up with Abbott and the Big Ten Conference for the We Give Blood Drive. The campaign ran during the 2024 college football season and ended with nearly 20,000 people donating blood.Brady shared the personal story in an interview with Axios. TB12 explained that blood donation had been part of his life since his school days.“I've been giving blood since I was in high school,” Brady told Axios.One statistic particularly caught his attention. “The one stat that stood out to me was every person that donates saves up to three lives,” he said in the same interview.Brady also made the process sound straightforward. “You just go there and spend an hour of your time and give something that can really help a lot of people in need,” he told Axios.That was the point he wanted fans to take away. People do not need to be professional athletes or wealthy donors to help someone. Giving blood is a practical way to support patients who need transfusions after accidents, during cancer treatment or following childbirth complications.Brady's involvement also came as the United States faced a serious blood shortage. On September 26, 2024, the American Red Cross reported an emergency shortage after donations dropped during the summer. The campaign aimed to bring more people, especially younger donors, into the process.Abbott and the Big Ten launched the We Give Blood Drive on September 26, 2024. The competition involved all 18 Big Ten universities, with students, alumni and fans donating blood in support of their chosen school.Each donation earned a point on the leaderboard. Abbott promised $1 million to the university that collected the most donations, with the money earmarked for student or community health projects.It gave college football fans another reason to back their school. Instead of cheering only for a win on Saturday, they could help their university climb the standings by donating blood.The competition ran through December 6, 2024, and Abbott announced the winner on December 7 at the Discover Big Ten Football Championship Game in Indianapolis.The University of Nebraska-Lincoln finished first and received the $1 million grant. Abbott reported that nearly 20,000 students, alumni and fans had donated blood during the campaign, potentially helping save as many as 60,000 lives.There was another encouraging result. Abbott said more than half of the donors at campus blood drives gave blood for the first time. That meant the campaign reached people who might not otherwise have considered donating.Brady did not need a football record to make his point. He brought attention to a habit he had kept since high school and helped connect it with a nationwide effort. The final numbers belonged to the thousands who showed up to donate, but his message was simple: an hour of your time could help someone who needs it.
Article Summary: The former New England Patriots quarterback teamed up with the Big Ten Conference and the American Red Cross for the We Give Blood Drive. The competition involved all 18 Big Ten universities, with students, alumni and fans donating blood in support of their chosen school. The University of Nebraska- Lincoln finished first and received the $1 million grant.

New Zealand have done their homework on India's teenage batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and are preparing specific plans to counter his explosive hitting, with pacer Jacob Duffy hoping home conditions will pose a fresh challenge for the 15-year-old ahead of the five-match T20I series beginning on Thursday.Sooryavanshi has taken the cricketing world by storm with his fearless approach and remarkable consistency, rewriting records in the Indian Premier League before becoming India's youngest international cricketer in the men's game with his T20I debut in England in July.After a quiet start to his international career against England, the left-handed opener announced himself on the global stage by smashing an 18-ball half-century against Zimbabwe, becoming the youngest player to score a fifty in men's international cricket. The five-match T20I series will provide an important test of his adaptability against an attack familiar with exploiting conditions at home.Duffy has already sounded out Hagley Oval's head groundsman about the surface and is hoping the pitch offers enough assistance to the bowlers to prevent a high-scoring contest."He's from Invercargill, so he's promised me a little bit of bounce," said Duffy, who was born in Lumsden, a small town near the South Island city. The Otago bowler won the Sir Richard Hadlee Medal as New Zealand's top player in 2025 and was part of Royal Challengers Bengaluru's IPL-winning campaign after reaching the final of the T20 World Cup earlier in the year.

Article Title: Who is Deepthi Jeevanji? Indian para-athlete wins 400m T20 gold with Games record
Article Text:

Who is Deepthi Jeevanji ?

From a village in Telangana to the international stage

What is the T20 category?

The role of her parents in her journey

NEW DELHI: Deepthi Jeevanji continued her impressive run in para athletics by winning gold in the women's 400m T20 event at the Asian Para Games on Tuesday. The Indian clocked a Games record time of 56.36 seconds to defend her title.The 23-year-old from Telangana finished ahead of Japan's Niina Kanno, who won silver in 58.92 seconds. Kanno's compatriot Akane Kato took bronze with a time of 1:00.26.Deepthi, who also holds the Asian record, has established herself as one of India's leading para-athletes with her performances at major international events.Deepthi hails from a remote village in Warangal, Telangana. Her parents are small farmers who have also worked as labourers in their village. Her talent for running was spotted when she was young. According to her athlete profile, Sports Authority of India coach N Ramesh first noticed her during a state-level athletics meet when she was 15. He recognised her potential and began training her.Deepthi later received support from badminton great Pullela Gopichand. At his suggestion, she underwent testing for intellectual disability in Hyderabad.Her journey in para athletics began to gain attention after she competed at the Asian Youth Championships in Hong Kong in 2019, where she won bronze.Deepthi continued to improve through competitions organised by the Athletics Federation of India between 2019 and 2022. She also won gold medals in the 100m and 200m events at the Khelo India Youth Games in Guwahati in 2020.Her breakthrough at the senior international level came at the Asian Para Games in 2023, where she won gold and set Games and Asian records in the women's 400m T20 event.She went on to win gold at the 2024 Para Athletics World Championships, setting a world record of 55.07 seconds. She also won a bronze medal in the same event at the Paris Paralympics in 2024.Deepthi added another achievement to her career by winning silver at the 2025 World Championships. She has also won gold at the Indian Open in 2025 and 2026.T20 is a classification for athletes with intellectual impairments. Athletes in this category may face challenges with processing information, concentration and following race plans or tactical strategies.Deepthi's success has come with strong support from her parents. She has spoken about how they stood by her ambitions even when people in their village taunted them for supporting her sporting dreams.Their support, along with years of training and hard work, has helped Deepthi rise from a village in Telangana to the top level of international para athletics.Her latest gold at the Asian Para Games, achieved in a Games record time of 56.36 seconds, is another milestone in her remarkable journey.
Article Summary: Deepthi Jeevanji won gold in the women's 400m T20 event at the Asian Para Games. The 23-year-old clocked a Games record time of 56.36 seconds to defend her title. She finished ahead of Japan's Niina Kanno, who won silver in 58.92 seconds.

Article Title: Asian Para Games 2026: Pradeep Kumar wins silver, Ayush Verma takes bronze in javelin
Article Text:
Pradeep Kumar (Image credit: ANI)

Iran's Erfan Bandori wins gold

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What is the Raza points system?

What are the F53 and F54 classifications?

India's Pradeep Kumar and Ayush Verma won silver and bronze medals respectively in the men's javelin throw F53/54 event at the Asian Para Games 2026 on Tuesday.Pradeep, competing in the F54 category, finished second with a personal best throw of 27.45 metres. It was his second successive silver medal at the Asian Para Games.Ayush, who competes in the F53 category, secured bronze with a throw of 17.88 metres. His performance earned him enough Raza points to finish on the podium.Iran's Erfan Bandori successfully defended his title with a Games record throw of 30.24 metres.Thailand's Sahar-dam Yaena finished behind Ayush despite throwing the javelin 23.31 metres. Ayush secured the higher position because the Raza points system takes the athletes' level of disability into account when different classifications compete in the same event.The Raza points system converts athletes' performances into scores based on their classification and level of disability. It allows athletes from different classifications to compete in the same event on a comparable basis.The F53 category is for athletes who have good arm and hand function but limited trunk control and no sitting balance because of reduced abdominal and lower back muscle function.The F54 category is for athletes who have good arm strength and some or full trunk muscle power, although their trunk and leg movements remain significantly affected.
Article Summary: Pradeep Kumar and Ayush Verma won silver and bronze medals respectively in the men's javelin throw F53/54 event at the Asian Para Games 2026. Iran's Erfan Bandori successfully defended his title with a Games record throw of 30.24 metres.

Actor Ignored Warnings

Tiger attack: 15 teams tracing shooters





MUMBAI: In yet another instance of a gangland attack on a film personality, unidentified motorcycle-borne assailants repeatedly fired at a car carrying actor Tiger Shroff and his driver Firdaus in Juhu around 7 pm Sunday, injuring Firdaus on his hand and a fan standing nearby who sustained bullet wounds near his chest.Seven shots were fired in all.
