He also rang Tiger Shroff and assured him saying, “We are all with you.”The incident took place barely 350 metres away from Juhu police station. The vehicle was slowly exiting the venue when two of the assailants, standing amidst a crowd of curious onlookers, sprang in front of the car and opened fire repeatedly.At least one bullet went through the shattered glass of the vehicle. Juhu police said the three assailants, in white shirts, fled in seconds towards SV Road and Vile Parle railway station on a bike kept idling by their accomplice.Also read: ‘Jaldi le kar jaao, Tiger’: Video shows seat switch as Tiger Shroff takes the wheel after attack Despite being injured, Shroff’s driver emerged from the vehicle and tried to chase them. A senior doctor at Nanavati Hospital, where Shroff and Firdaus were taken, said initial scans showed a foreign body lodged in the latter’s left hand as a result of a bullet injury. He is likely to undergo surgery.In a purported video going viral on social media, one of the two shooters appears unable to fire when he is closest to the car window. The gun seemingly jams as he prepares to fire a sixth shot at point-blank range.Police were registering an FIR and seeking details from actor Tiger Shroff about any recent threat calls or warnings after unidentified motorcycle-borne assailants repeatedly fired at his car on Sunday. Fifteen teams have been formed to trace the assailants. Juhu police and Mumbai crime branch officers were examining CCTV footage to identify them and establish their escape route.Also Read: ‘Should focus on actual criminals’: Dipke jabs police after shots fired at Tiger Shroff “Shroff only has minor abrasions,” said a senior doctor at Nanavati Hospital. The actor was in the hospital’s emergency room till the time of going to the press, awaiting doctor’s advice on his discharge and the treatment plan for his driver.The third person injured in the firing—a passerby identified by police as 35-year-old Umesh Charan—sustained bullet injuries on the right side of his chest, according to Dr Chhaya Shinde, dean of BMC-run Cooper Hospital in Juhu. “He is stable at the moment but will need immediate surgery,” said a doctor.In a press release, BMC said the third patient arrived at the Cooper Hospital casualty at 7.10pm with a “history of a gunshot wound sustained at 6.30pm at Vile Parle West while covering a football match featuring Tiger Shroff. “The patient came with an entry wound at 2cm below left nipple,” the release added.Also Read: ‘Jaldi le kar jaao, Tiger’: Video shows actor taking wheel after attack Police initially said Shroff suffered slight abrasions from glass fragments after the car’s windows shattered, but DCP (west zone 2) Mohit Garg said the actor was not injured.Meanwhile, the Lawrence Bishnoi gang claimed responsibility on social media for the attack. The message concluded with threats directed at rival gang members and was accompanied by several hashtags referencing the Lawrence Bishnoi group and other affiliated associate networks. Article Title: Fragments of Halley’s Comet, which comes after every 76 years, to light up the night sky this week: All you need to know
Article Text:
Orionid Meteor Shower Peaks October 21–22

When and how to watch the Orionids

Other key planetary events this week

Viewing advice for stargazing

Skywatchers are in for an autumn celestial treat this week as debris from arguably the solar system's most famous cosmic visitor, Halley's Comet, streaks across the night sky in the annual Orionid meteor shower. While the comet itself only visits the inner solar system once every 76 years, tiny fragments left trailing in its ancient orbital path will collide with Earth's atmosphere, vaporizing into fast-moving “shooting stars.” Alongside the meteor shower, the stargazing calendar from Monday, October 19 through Sunday, October 25 features major planetary movements, including Venus transitioning between morning and evening skies and a close encounter between a bright waxing moon and Saturn.The Orionids reach their peak activity overnight from Wednesday, October 21 into Thursday, October 22, capable of producing up to 20 shooting stars per hour under dark, clear skies, as per a report in Forbes. Notably, the prime viewing hours occur in the late overnight window just before dawn. The bright moon will set before the pre-dawn hours, leaving the sky dark right when the constellation Orion stands high overhead and North America directly faces the incoming debris stream.In addition to the meteor display, skywatchers should circle Saturday, October 24 for two major planetary highlights. The first is Venus at Inferior Conjunction. On Saturday, Venus passes directly between the Earth and the Sun, officially ending its long presence as the brilliant “Evening Star.” While it will be completely lost in the Sun's glare on Saturday, Venus will emerge over the coming weeks in the eastern dawn sky to begin its cycle as the “Morning Star. ”The Moon Meets Saturn: Also on Saturday evening, if you glance toward the southeast immediately after sunset, a 94%-lit waxing gibbous moon will appear in close proximity to Saturn. While the ringed planet sits a few weeks past its opposition, it remains easily visible to the naked eye and presents an outstanding view through backyard telescopes.As a bright moon dominates much of the week, faint deep-sky targets will be difficult to spot. Observers are advised to focus instead on prominent winter constellations. For example, the northeast sky will have “W” formation of Cassiopeia, with the cascading star stream of Perseus resting directly below it.Later in the evening, watch for the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters cluster) rising ahead of Taurus the Bull and its reddish anchor star, Aldebaran. Followed shortly after is Orion, recognized by its three iconic belt stars rising almost vertically from the horizon.
Article Summary: The Orionid meteor shower will peak overnight from Wednesday, October 21 into Thursday, October 22. On Saturday, Venus passes directly between the Earth and the Sun, officially ending its long presence as the brilliant “Evening Star.” On Saturday evening, a 94%-lit waxing gibbous moon will appear in close proximity to Saturn.

Article Title: In 2001, a former Illinois quarry where solvents and paint were dumped opened as a forest preserve with a 115-acre lake, an education centre, and an amphitheatre
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image. Credits - Gemini

From gravel pit to disposal site

Checking the site

AI-generated representative image. Credits - Gemini

Creating the lake and the preserve

Old gravel pits are a common sight in the American Midwest. When the sand and stone are exhausted, they often are left as deep pits with steep walls, and some of them silently turn into dumping places. It’s not often you get a second life as a spot where families swim, rent boats and set up on a lawn for summer concerts.That’s what happened at the former Petersen Sand and Gravel quarry in Libertyville, Lake County, Illinois. Once the barrels of paint and solvent waste were excavated and hauled away and the federal and state agencies decided no additional cleanup was necessary, the Lake County Forest Preserve District completed the conversion of the pit into Independence Grove Forest Preserve. It opened to the public in spring 2001 with a lake of 115 acres, a visitor centre and an amphitheatre.According to an EPA fact sheet on reuse, the quarry was in operation from 1952 to 1971. By the time it closed, much of the topsoil was gone, and the sides had vertical walls of up to 60 feet high. It would be a tough place to adore, but the Lake County Forest Preserve District purchased the area in 1979 and began designing a preserve around it.The pit’s darker history began when its owner, Raymond Petersen, let people deposit waste in a worked-out corner from the mid-1950s, state records show. Nobody knows when the paint, the paint debris and the solvents started coming. Petersen was refused a permit for a landfill in 1971, and the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency investigated allegations of illegal dumping and ordered it stopped. Between 400 and 500 drums of paint and solvent waste were removed in 1977.Later, there were more. Lake County Grading, the mining firm the district had contracted to regrade the pit in exchange for the remaining gravel, found hidden drums while regrading in 1983. That year, a forest preserve district contractor removed contaminated soil and about 500 drums of solvents and 1,000 paint cans.The pit was included on the federal Superfund National Priorities List in 1986, and the Illinois EPA, with help from the US EPA, conducted a detailed examination. Fieldwork was carried out between October 1986 and December 1987, with the final report submitted in April 1988. Investigators took samples of groundwater, soil, surface water and sediment. They analysed groundwater for more than 150 compounds, and only iron and manganese went above drinking water guidelines set for taste and odour, a level that was also exceeded in groundwater upgradient of the site. Soil showed low levels of a few solvents, such as toluene, plus traces of pesticides and one low reading of PCBs.Investigators were also keen to make sure no more drums were hidden. They took soil borings at the three known dumping areas and 23 other locations and did buried metal surveys over a 20-acre grid. Nothing came up.A 1988 EPA document summed up the findings: the earlier waste removals had been enough to protect people and the environment, and no unacceptable danger remained, so no further cleanup was required. There was one requirement. Because no one could accurately predict conditions once a lake filled the pit, the agencies asked the county to monitor surface water and sediment before and after the lake was formed. The facility was removed off the Superfund list in 1991.The district signed an agreement with Lake County Grading to regrade and restore the property in exchange for mining the remaining gravel. What began as plans for walks, picnicking, swimming and boating expanded to include a visitor centre, a marina complex, a cafe, an event pavilion, an amphitheatre and a native plant garden. While mining continued, crews pumped around 1.7 million gallons of water a night from a sump pond into the neighbouring Des Plaines River to keep the pit dry. The pit floor sat about 20 feet below the river level, so it had to be pumped dry for mining to continue.When the work was done, the 120-acre former quarry site formed part of a forest preserve of more than 1,100 acres, centred on a 115-acre lake. The visitor centre covers 19,000 square feet and hosts changing exhibits. The preserve also features a marina with boat rentals, a beach, catch-and-release fishing, miles of trails and guided night hikes with naturalists. The amphitheatre hosts an annual summer concert series next to a fountain and native garden.As of 2007, the site had not had any further environmental problems since it was redeveloped, and a visitor would be hard-pressed to tell that the lake sits in a former quarry and garbage dumping area, the fact sheet says. The lesson from Libertyville is not that of a magical cleanup but of patience, testing and monitoring that allowed a ruined gravel pit to become a lake that visitors today use for swimming, boating and fishing.

Article Title: Why has Shafali Verma been reprimanded by the ICC after India's win over Zimbabwe?
Article Text:
Shafali Verma (BCCI Photo)

What happened during the match?

One demerit point added to her record

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What is the penalty for a Level 1 breach ?

India vice-captain Shafali Verma has received an official reprimand for throwing the ball to the ground in frustration after dropping a catch during the second T20I against Zimbabwe.The incident took place during India's nine-wicket win in Raipur on Sunday. The 22-year-old was found guilty of breaching Level 1 of the ICC Code of Conduct.The incident took place in the 12th over of Zimbabwe's innings. Shafali dropped a catch offered by Chipo Mugeri-Tiripano at mid-off off Shree Charani's bowling. She then threw the ball to the ground in frustration.The ICC found that Shafali had breached Article 2.2 of its Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel. This rule deals with the “abuse of cricket equipment or clothing, ground equipment or fixtures and fittings during an International Match,” an ICC media release said.Along with the official reprimand, one demerit point has been added to Shafali's disciplinary record. This was her first offence in a 24-month period.Shafali admitted the offence and accepted the sanction proposed by G.S. Lakshmi of the ICC International Panel of Match Referees.As a result, there was no need for a formal hearing.On-field umpires Vrinda Rathi and Gayathri Venugopalan, third umpire Anna Harris and fourth umpire Janani Narayanan levelled the charge.Level 1 breaches of the ICC Code of Conduct carry a minimum penalty of an official reprimand. The maximum punishment is a fine of 50 per cent of a player's match fee, along with one or two demerit points.

Article Title: Meet Cliver Huamán: At 15, turned away from South America’s biggest club soccer final, he climbed a hill, called the match and drew thousands of live viewers
Article Text:
Cliver Huamán traveled to Estadio Monumental in Lima, Peru to narrate the match but livestreamed from a nearby hillside after he could not enter the stadium. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Cliver Huamán began narrating matches online about four years before the 2025 final

He traveled 16 to 18 hours and was unable to get accreditation for the November 29, 2025 final

Reports put his peak concurrent audience between 10,000 and 47,000 viewers

Live streaming research offers context for the audience he reached

Who Watches Live Streaming in China? Examining Viewers’ Behaviors, Personality Traits, and Motivations

The Puruchuco archaeological site in Lima. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Motivations for the Use of Video Game Streaming Platforms: The Moderating Effect of Sex, Age and Self-Perception of Level as a Player

Television invitations in Lima and Madrid followed the broadcast

Many of the biggest games in South American football draw far more spectators outside the stadiums than inside them. Fans watch on television and radio and, increasingly, on social media, where anyone with a mobile phone and a microphone can build an audience. One such commentator is Cliver Huamán Sánchez, a teenager from Huampica, in the Andes of Peru, who narrates football matches online under the name Pol Deportes. For the Copa Libertadores final in Lima, he travelled from his home region to cover the match live. He was not allowed into the stadium and instead narrated it from a nearby hill.Cliver Huamán Sánchez, from Huampica in Andahuaylas, Peru, began posting match videos online about four years before the 2025 final, Caretas reported. His older brother, Kenny, persuaded him to build his own channels, and his father had taken him to a local radio station as a child, according to a BBC Mundo interview republished by Observador in Costa Rica. Bluewin, a Swiss news site, adds that the family grows kiwicha and quinoa.According to a December 1, 2025 TUDN report, Cliver Huamán could not get press credentials for the Copa Libertadores final because he was 15 and not yet an adult.Reports differ on the length of the trip from Andahuaylas: Reuters and We Are Mitú give 18 hours, while Bluewin and BBC Mundo give 16 hours. NTN24 reported that Flamengo won 1–0 against Palmeiras at the Estadio Monumental in Lima on November 29, 2025, winning the Copa Libertadores. Huamán climbed Cerro Puruchuco, an Inca archaeological site east of Lima, as El País describes it. El Litoral and NTN24 report that he set up a phone, ring light, tripod and microphone, put on a suit and tie, and streamed live on TikTok while his brother produced.FutbolPeruano.com reports that he provided commentary for the full 90 minutes and drew an audience of 47,000, along with more than one million followers. Ecuador’s Extra reported on December 3, 2025 that Huamán described his livestream growing from 30 viewers to 400, then 5,000 and then 10,000. Estimates of his audience therefore range from 10,000 concurrent viewers to 47,000 at peak.A 2020 study of live-streaming viewers in China offers some context for the audience he reached, although it does not cover football in Latin America. In, published in Frontiers in Psychology , Yi Xu and Yixin Ye identified social interaction, information gathering, and entertainment as the main motivations for watching live streams, and found that those motivations were linked to how often viewers watched and which genres they chose. Extraversion was negatively associated with live streaming use, while openness was positively associated.A second paper,, appeared in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health . In the study, the authors modelled 338 valid responses and found that the three motivation constructs explained 70.8% of the variance in use, with an SRMR below 0.10 indicating acceptable fit. They also report that sex and age did not moderate the motivation- use relationship, whereas self-perceived player level did, so hypotheses 4 and 5 were rejected.L1 MAX, which holds the broadcasting rights for the Sporting Cristal-Alianza Lima playoff, invited Huamán to narrate part of the match at Lima’s Estadio Nacional, Panamericana reported. Latina Television then invited him to travel to Spain to cover the Champions League match between Real Madrid and Manchester City, We Are Mitú reported, and Caretas says he hopes to win a scholarship to study journalism and communication.
Article Summary: Cliver Huamán Sánchez, from Huampica in Andahuaylas, Peru, began posting match videos online about four years before the 2025 final. He was unable to get press credentials for the Copa Libertadores final because he was 15 and not yet an adult. He travelled from his home region to cover the match live but was not allowed into the stadium and instead narrated it from a nearby hill.

Article Title: ‘I’m playing better now’: Stefanos Tsitsipas on father-coach split, pressure and his tennis revival
Article Text:
Stefanos Tsitsipas (Getty Images)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

ALMATY: Stefanos Tsitsipas folded his 6 ft 4’ frame into a sofa in a busy corridor at the Almaty Open.The 28-year-old, once ranked as high as No. 3 in the world and now at No. 39, acknowledged that his road back began with letting go. Letting go of the pressure, the tension and the expectations that have weighed on him. And, most importantly, allowing his father to be a father again, rather than having to be both father and coach.Tsitsipas, who finished in the Top-10 for five consecutive years, from 2019 to 2023, believes he is playing better tennis now than he was a few years ago, when he reached two Grand Slam finals, at Roland Garros in 2021 and the Australian Open in 2023.The dip in form began with his body, a back problem that had been troubling him for some time, compounded by a strained coaching relationship with his father, Apostolos. The combination took its toll on his confidence, and by June his ranking had plummeted to No. 88.Just before Wimbledon, Tsitsipas told Greek media that he was ending his professional relationship with his father for good.“I love my father, and I love him as a father,” he said in Almaty.“I want to keep the professional part out of my relationship with my father. My relationship with him has improved now that he’s not my coach. It was very difficult for me to separate the coach and the father. I had reached a point where I could not avoid being triggered.”“We’re still in touch, and I really like the way things are right now,” he added.That separation appears to have given Tsitsipas something he had been missing, room to breathe. The weight of expectation and the tension of a relationship complicated by professional demands had produced disturbing scenes at tennis tournaments around the world, a father in his fifties hurling instructions at his son, sometimes leading to heated exchanges between the two.“Eliminating the pressure factor does help,” he told TOI at the Almaty Open. “Before, I felt pressured a lot of the time. There were a lot of things piled up within me, and certain people triggered me in a negative way. Removing some of those triggers, and having people around me who keep me calm and help me be more forgiving (on myself) when things don't work out, allows me to experiment more and not be afraid to try things. ”For Tsitsipas, that freedom is essential for growth.“When you feel judged, you tend to go for the safe options. And safety is not always where growth is. You need a team that isn't going to judge you for what you do, but will analyse it and support you, because it's all part of the process.”The numbers suggest that the process is beginning to pay off. Across his first 16 events of the season, Tsitsipas went 16-14. In the 10 tournaments since Wimbledon, he has gone 21-8, winning the title in Gstaad in July to end a 16-month drought.Now working with Thomas Perrin, and with Patrick Mouratoglou overseeing the process, he believes his tennis is better than it has been in years.“I'm playing better now than I played a few years back,” he said.“I feel like I was kind of stuck in the past. Certain aspects of my game weren't properly structured, and there wasn't really a base to build on.”Since August, he has beaten Arthur Fils, No. 11 (then ranked), Jiri Lehecka, No. 19, Tomas Etcheverry, No. 30, Luciano Darderi 21, and Taylor Fritz, No. 12.One of the most revealing signs of that progress concerns his backhand. One of only three players in the top 50 to use a single-handed backhand, alongside Lorenzo Musetti and Denis Shapovalov, Tsitsipas has increasingly found opponents targeting that side of the court.“My backhand is probably even better than my forehand right now. I've played some really good matches and used it as an actual weapon on court. Against (Daniil) Medvedev recently, I used it to approach the net, slice, change pace and rhythm, play down the line and open up the court. There's more variety now, whereas before it felt like one-way traffic.”Range matters. Tsitsipas knows opponents will continue to target his backhand, but he feels better equipped to respond, using changes of pace, depth and direction to keep them guessing rather than allowing them to dictate play.For Tsitsipas, the way forward is about rediscovering the freedom to play on his own terms, with a clearer mind and a game he believes in again.
Article Summary: Stefanos Tsitsipas says he is playing better tennis now than he did a few years ago. The 28-year-old was once ranked as high as No. 3 in the world and now at No. 39. He has been working with Thomas Perrin, and with Patrick Mouratoglou overseeing the process.

Article Title: Mumbai woman threatened to circulate video recordings, extorted Rs 4 crore from jeweller
Article Text:
(AI image) A 40-year-old woman named Naznin Mehmood was arrested for extorting Rs 4 crore from a jewellery shop owner

MUMBAI:





A 40-year-old woman has been arrested by the city Crime Branch for allegedly extorting nearly Rs 4 crore from a 61-year-old jewellery shop owner by threatening to circulate video recordings of him watching her while she undressed or bathed. Unit 7 of the Crime Branch arrested Naznin Mehmood, a resident of VP Road in south Mumbai.According to the police, the accused became acquainted with the complainant through visits to the jewellery shop where he worked. The two exchanged mobile numbers and remained in contact. The complainant alleged that she subsequently recorded video calls and used the recordings to blackmail him.The alleged extortion continued from February 2025 to August 2026, during which the complainant claimed to have paid approximately Rs 4 crore in cash and through online transactions. The accused allegedly told him that the recordings had reached the Chennai Police and other authorities and demanded money to have them deleted or prevent their circulation.The woman initially sought money, claiming that she needed to settle the matter with the police. She subsequently allegedly claimed that payments had to be made to court officials, senior police officers and other authorities to ensure that the recordings were deleted.The complainant alleged that he raised money by selling gold and making payments in instalments. He also claimed that the woman threatened to break his hands and legs and kill him if he failed to meet her demands. Even after he had paid Rs 4 crore, the woman allegedly demanded another Rs 15 lakh, threatening to visit his residence and workplace and circulate the recordings online if he failed to pay by October 18, the complaint stated.Acting on his complaint, the Crime Branch team laid a trap and arrested Naznin. The police are investigating how the alleged extortion proceeds were collected and where the money went. Investigators are also verifying the complainant’s claim that he paid approximately Rs 4 crore over several months, including through online transactions.The role of any other persons who may have assisted the accused, as well as the authenticity of her claims that the police and other authorities possessed the recordings, is also under investigation.
Article Summary: A 40-year-old woman named Naznin Mehmood was arrested for extorting Rs 4 crore from a jewellery shop owner. She allegedly threatened to circulate video recordings of him watching her while she undressed or bathed. The alleged extortion continued from February 2025 to August 2026.

Article Title: 9 injured after fire breaks out on 12th floor of high-rise building in Mumbai
Article Text:
(Representative image) fire ignited on the 12th floor of the Kohinoor HDIL Building No. 6 in Kurla West, causing injuries to nine people, including a five-year-old boy and two teenagers





MUMBAI: Nine people, including a five-year-old boy, were injured after a fire broke out on the 12th floor of a high-rise building in Kurla West on Tuesday morning.The fire was reported at 6.53am at Kohinoor HDIL Building No. 6, near Kohinoor Hospital. According to the Mumbai Fire Brigade (MFB), the blaze broke out on the 12th floor and was extinguished at 7.21am.Eight people suffered suffocation due to smoke inhalation and were admitted to Rajawadi Hospital. A ninth person, a 55-year-old man, sustained an injury to his right leg. All nine were reported to be in stable condition.Among those injured were a five-year-old boy, a 14-year-old girl and a 17-year-old girl. The injured also included adults aged between 18 and 65.The Mumbai Fire Brigade, police, Adani personnel, a 108 ambulance team and civic ward staff were mobilised to the spot. Further details about the cause of the fire have yet to be established.
Article Summary: The fire was reported at 6.53am at Kohinoor HDIL Building No. 6 in Kurla West. The blaze broke out on the 12th floor and was extinguished at 7.21am. Among those injured were a five-year-old boy and two teenagers. All nine were reported to be in stable condition.

Article Title: Move over celebrity hotspots, Mumbai's courtroom 55 is where Bollywood’s brush with Lawrence Bishnoi gang plays out
Article Text:
For those tracking Bollywood's uneasy brush with the gangland network of Lawrence Bishnoi, this is the arena where the famous meet the infamous.

Scaling pipes, just to see a bit of Salman in court





MUMBAI: Until recently, celebrity-spotters hoping to catch a glimpse of film stars would stake out Bandra Bandstand, Juhu or Film City in the suburbs. The hunt has now taken an unexpected turn to south Mumbai-to Courtroom No. 55, tucked away on the fifth floor of a building in the city civil and sessions court complex in Kala Ghoda.For those tracking Bollywood's uneasy brush with the gangland network of Lawrence Bishnoi, this is the arena where the famous meet the infamous.Presided over by special judge Satyanarayan Ramjivan Navandar, the court is hearing a cluster of cases linked to the Lawrence gang under the Maharashtra Control of Organized Crime Act (MCOCA). The list includes alleged firing outside actor Salman Khan's Bandra residence and filmmaker Rohit Shetty's home, and the murder of politician Baba Siddique who had ties with Bollywood's elite. If MCOCA is invoked in the attack on actor Tiger Shroff, that matter too could find its way here.It was the Salman Khan case hearings that first brought the chamber into the spotlight. He is expected to appear as a key witness along with his brother, actor-producer Arbaaz.It was on the same building's fourth floor in Courtroom No 52 that Salman was sentenced to 5 years in jail for running over four people and killing one in 2002 (he was acquitted by Bombay high court). His repeated appearances over 2 years then drew large crowds.Among regular visitors was Pranita Fulsagar from Pune who travelled four hours for every hearing. Now married to a cop and mother to twins, Fulsagar, 32, is hoping to see the actor in person again. "I have a book full of his pictures," she said. "I want him to live a full and happy life," she said.Quiet courtrooms in the City Civil and Sessions Court complex have often been dramatically transformed during sensational trials into packed spaced filled with lawyers, litigants, court staff and curious onlookers. They make up a motley bunch. One frequent attendee at Salman’s last trial was a senior citizen from Bandra, who took notes with coloured pens and claimed he had been at the accident spot on the night of the incident. For the Salman Khan case of 2002, the day of the judgment in May 2015 was marked by special arrangements.Entry to the fourth-floor courtroom was cordoned off, and people scaled the building opposite the court using water pipelines to catch a glimpse of Khan through the courtroom window. Court staff fear a repeat of the dangerous climb, this time a floor higher, when Khan arrives to depose in the MCOCA trial. Threats received by the actor from the Bishnoi network culminated in the firing outside his home on Apr 14, 2024 and triggered a major investigation into organised crime rackets operating across states.The Baba Siddique case has added a graver dimension. Siddique was shot dead outside his son’s office in Bandra (E) on Oct 12, 2024. Police linked the murder to Bishnoi-led organised crime activity. The tone in court around such a case is sombre. Even in a room used to high-profile name-dropping, a murder trial changes the atmosphere. There is less whispering, more note-taking, and a constant reminder that behind every “sensational case” is a dead man, a grieving family and a prosecution required to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.The Rohit Shetty case has added to the impression that Courtroom 55 is the place where cases involving alleged gang threats to Bollywood are heard. Now, with reports that the Tiger Shroff case may be tried under MCOCA, Courtroom No 55 could see another high-profile number. MCOCA cases are not routine assignments, they require allegations of organised crime activity, prior offences, continuing unlawful activity and sanction from the authorities.If that threshold is crossed, Courtroom No 55 could be assigned with hearing more such remands. Yet despite the celebrity backdrop, everyday life inside 55 remains rooted in bureaucratic reality. Known for maintaining a strict, no-nonsense courtroom, Judge Navandar delivers sharp judicial remarks when police procedure falters.When investigators recently faced difficulty securing physical custody of Anmol Bishnoi, the judge pulled up the Crime Branch for showing little effort and asked why video conferencing had not been used if transfer orders were stuck in red tape. In 55, celebrity, box-office success and gangster notoriety carry little weight if the paperwork is not in order.
Article Summary: Courtroom No. 55 is tucked away on the fifth floor of a building in the city civil and sessions court complex in Kala Ghoda. The court is hearing a cluster of cases linked to the Lawrence gang under the Maharashtra Control of Organized Crime Act (MCOCA) The list includes alleged firing outside actor Salman Khan's Bandra residence and filmmaker Rohit Shetty's home.

Article Title: ​​Sambhajinagar set to celebrate Dasara today
Article Text:
Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar

:





As Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar was in full festive mode on the eve of the Dasara festival on Monday, markets in Gulmandi, Shahgunj, Aurangpura and Cidco bustled with shoppers buying new clothes and booking vehicles among other activities. Electronics stores also reported bookings for delivery, as the day is considered auspicious for new beginnings.Flower vendors reported heavy demand for marigold garlands even though the flowers fetched a low price of around Rs40 per kg for sellers.The festival of Dasara, which marks the victory of good over evil and concludes the Navaratra festival, will be celebrated with Shastra Puja during Vijay Muhurat in the afternoon and Ravana dahan after sunset. Many families will perform Seemollanghan and exchange “apta” leaves as gold during the evening.“Dasara festival is a time to seek blessings of Goddess Durga and family elders and relatives. The festive occasion facilitates brief reunion of friends and relatives, which is an added joy,” Shubhada Kulkarni, an entrepreneur, said.The burning of the effigy of demon king Ravana has been scheduled at Ram Lila ground, CIDCO N-7 and HUDCO N-11 and Waluj among other areas of Sambhajinagar on Tuesday evening.At N-11 HUDCO, the highlight will be the tableaux of Lord Ram, Sita, Lakshman and an 11-foot Hanuman, accompanied by a 100-member ‘Vanar Sena’ of children and volunteers, according to organisers.
